source.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization via Bregman Bias-Variance Decomposition
source.authors: Geng-Ze Xu; Wei Yao; Zi-Qiao Wang; Yong Liu

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some figures are garbled in the text extraction, so their exact plotted values cannot be read.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical sufficient conditions for weak-to-strong generalization and reports empirical results on student size, teacher ensembles, and training losses. Its findings refine the claim: the theory is conditional, and increasing student size does not necessarily maximize the empirical gain.
record.gate_note: The paper does not report PGR values. Table 1 reports student test accuracy by training loss and teacher–student pair, but not the weak teacher's test accuracy. Figure 1 and Figure 3 provide qualitative size and ensemble findings; their plotted values are not legible in the extraction. The paper also reports ImageNet student accuracies, but does not provide teacher-versus-student comparisons there, so those results do not establish the vision version. Results cited from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper derives sufficient conditions under which a student beats its weak teacher (V5). It also runs weak-to-strong experiments with GPT-2 and Qwen teacher–student pairs, comparing teacher ensembles with single teachers and comparing loss variants (CE, RCE, AUX, CACE, SL) on the student's accuracy or loss (V2, V3). It never reports the weak teacher's test accuracy or PGR, so its experiments cannot show the basic effect (V1). T2 fits better than T5: the paper offers a new analysis and method aimed at the same question, and does not argue that a version is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that the student approximating its posterior-mean teacher is sufficient for W2SG, and that larger students can achieve this (proved for ridge regression). They add that gain is not monotonic in size and that lower student entropy favours W2SG. RCE is more robust than CE to uncertain labels, and the hybrid losses (CACE or SL) consistently beat CE, RCE and AUX.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the weak-teacher pseudo-label and strong-student fine-tuning setup, with full fine-tuning and task-specific heads. It studies Bregman risk and compares CE, RCE, CACE, SL, AUX, and teacher ensembles; it does not report the original PGR measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with student size, teacher ensemble versus individual-teacher supervision, loss choice, task, and teacher-label confidence. The authors report non-monotonic gains with student size and especially strong RCE robustness at low confidence.

fits_no_version.finding: In knowledge distillation (strong teacher to weak student), RCE keeps higher accuracy than CE on low-confidence labels (Figure 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RCE's robustness to uncertain soft labels holds outside weak-to-strong settings.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306 (as stated in the text)
record.problems: No PGR values are reported. Table 1 omits weak-teacher accuracies and reports best outcomes selected from hyperparameter settings; error bars or confidence intervals are not stated there. Several central size and confidence comparisons rely on figures whose exact values are unreadable in the extracted text. The empirical results use at least three seeds, but uncertainty estimates are not given for the Table 1 values.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 also gives RCE, AUX, and SL results for the same 12 teacher–student/dataset combinations; these separate loss results were omitted to prioritize CE-versus-CACE comparisons and the other claim versions. Additional CACE/SL results in Table 3 and qualitative CE/RCE plots in Figures 3, 5–8 were not separately extracted.

untested.parts: No weak-teacher accuracy or loss is reported next to the student results, and no PGR is computed. The empirical basic effect cannot be read from this study.
Chess, and predictors of PGR such as representations. Size effects are given only as student loss, not PGR.
ImageNet AlexNet→ResNet-50/ViT student accuracies are given (Table 3) without teacher accuracy, so the effect itself is not shown.

missing.what: RCE, AUX and SL accuracies for all 12 teacher–student/dataset pairs. RCE is below CE on all three CAI-Harmless Qwen pairs.
Amazon Polarity Qwen pairs (CACE 96.5–97.1 vs CE 95.5–96.4). ImageNet AlexNet→ResNet-50/ViT-B/8: CE 61.70/66.68, CACE 61.70/70.03, RCE 44.67/54.63. No teacher accuracy is given.
Twitter Sentiment bias–variance size sweep with ensemble vs single teacher (figure-only).

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 numbers are single values: CACE, SL and AUX are each the best of several hyperparameter settings, while CE is untuned, and no error bars are shown. No weak-teacher accuracy appears anywhere, so no empirical result shows the student beating the teacher or allows PGR. Small CACE margins should be read with this selection advantage in mind.

versions.untested_parts: No PGR is calculated, and the empirical tables do not report the weak supervisor's accuracy alongside the student's. The empirical evidence therefore does not quantify the recovered performance gap.
The study compares CE, RCE, AUX, CACE, and SL, but the extracted rows focus on CE versus CACE. It does not report PGR for these loss comparisons.

The study tests student scaling in GPT-2 and Qwen settings, uses NLP and reward-modeling tasks, and analyzes a ridge-regression setting. It does not test chess or analyze what predicts PGR as defined in the claim.
No test of students exploiting weaknesses the teacher cannot check, distribution shift, or gains shrinking when teacher and student errors are alike.
Theoretical sufficient conditions are analyzed, but the paper does not establish a general necessity result that a student must beat its supervisor.
ImageNet results are reported for weak-to-strong training objectives, but no teacher-versus-student result establishes the weak-to-strong effect outside language.

rows.subject: Bregman bias–variance framework (Theorem 4.1)
rows.operation_detail: Derives a population-risk inequality for teacher and student under a Bregman divergence.

conditions.value: Joint expectation over data and teacher–student parameter randomness

rows.measure: Expected student population risk relative to teacher risk and reverse misfit
rows.value: Student risk ≤ teacher risk − expected reverse misfit + ϵ1; the paper states W2SG follows when ϵ1 is sufficiently small.
rows.note: A conditional theoretical bound, not an empirical measurement or a PGR estimate.
rows.check: A theoretical bound, not an empirical test of V1, so the V1 link is removed. As a V5 result it states the condition (small ϵ1) under which the student beats the teacher.

rows.subject: Bregman bias–variance framework (Corollary 4.1)
rows.operation_detail: Derives an equality for risk when the student matches the teacher's conditional posterior mean.

conditions.value: Student predictions equal the conditional expectation of teacher predictions given the student

rows.value: The residual vanishes and student risk equals teacher risk minus the expected divergence between the conditional-mean teacher and teacher.
rows.note: The paper presents this as a sufficient condition; it does not claim the condition is necessary.
rows.check: A theoretical sufficient condition; it bears on V5, not on the empirical basic effect (V1).

rows.subject: Ridge regression student (Example 1)
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes an overparameterized ridge-regression student as student capacity increases.
rows.measure: Expected squared misfit between trained student and teacher
rows.value: E∥fW′(X) − fW(X)∥² → B(1 − γ2) as n, ds, dw → ∞; the paper states the misfit decreases monotonically in γ1 up to an o(1) error.
rows.note: This is a theoretical asymptotic result in a ridge-regression example, not a measured PGR.
rows.check: In the ridge example, misfit converges to a positive constant and decreases with student width as the theorem states. Marking it partial understated the derived result.

rows.subject: Ridge regression student (Corollary 5.2)
rows.operation_detail: Shows the residual tends to zero as the ridge-regression student becomes sufficiently large.
rows.measure: Residual ϵ2 in the squared-loss risk bound
rows.value: ϵ2 → 0; together with the positive limiting misfit B(1 − γ2), the paper concludes that W2SG emerges in this setting.
rows.note: The result supports a conditional theoretical claim for the stated regression setting.
rows.check: A theoretical result in the ridge-regression setting, not an empirical V1 test, so the V1 link is removed.
